title: Chapter 32 – Nine Bells
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Wenyuan]

On the hundredth morning, Lin Wenyuan rings the bell nine times.

It is not heavy work. The bell in the ancestral hall is bronze and old and hangs low enough for a child to reach, and the rope is soft with a century of Patriarchs' hands. But he stands under it for a long moment before he pulls, with the whole house gathered in the cold courtyard behind him, and his left hand will not stop shaking.

Not from weakness. The hand is steadier than it has been in ten years. It shakes because for the first time in a hundred days he is allowed to lift it, and his father is not there to tell him which stroke comes first.

One. The sound rolls out over the roofs and down the terraces. Two. Somewhere below the wall a dog begins to bark and stops. Three, four. He counts the way his father counted, slowly, so that each stroke has time to finish before the next one starts. At nine the last note hangs in the frosty air over Green Pine Hill and thins out into nothing, and the mourning is over.

Behind him, forty-one people let out a breath together. He does not turn around. He lays his palm flat on the cold bronze until the humming stops under it.

"It is done, Father," he says, too softly for anyone to hear. "I will sit in the chair now."

* * *

The Patriarch's study smells of pine soot, camphor and old paper, and for a hundred days it has smelled of nothing at all, because the door was sealed.

That is the custom. For a hundred days after a Patriarch's death the study stays shut, the brush rests on its stand, and the seal of the house is locked in its box. The clan runs on what is already written. Third Aunt Wenqing kept the herb gardens going, Fourth Uncle Wenshi kept the guard on the walls, and Elder Aunt Lin Wenjun kept the small daily accounts in a notebook that she carried against her chest like a baby. Nothing larger was decided. Wenyuan had the sword and the funeral and the duty of being seen. He did not have the chair.

He breaks the paper seal on the door with his thumb. The paper is Jian's paper, smooth and fine-grained, the kind that was never made on this hill ten years ago. He notices that now, and puts the thought away.

The chair is plain black wood with a worn dent in the left arm where Lin Zhenshan rested his sword hand for forty years. Wenyuan sits in it. It is too wide for him, and for a moment he feels like a boy again, caught playing in the wrong room.

"You will get used to it," Lin Wenjun says from the doorway. "Everyone says so. I have not noticed that anyone ever does."

She has already set the ledgers on the desk in four neat stacks. Wenjun is sixty, small and gray-haired and sharp, and she came to the clan accounts from the side branch after Wenhai's confession because there was no one else the council would trust with a pen. She does not look rested. She has spent most of the hundred days quietly taking Wenhai's books apart.

"Sit," Wenyuan says. "Please. I would rather not read these alone."

"You would rather not read them at all." She sits, and opens the top ledger to a page marked with a strip of red cloth. "But you will, so let me save you the first hour. Here is the autumn quarter. Income from the shop at Willow Ford, from the terraces, from the Mirror Guard contract, from the guard's escort work, from everything we sell. One hundred and four low stones."

Wenyuan waits for the rest of the sentence.

"That is all of it," Wenjun says. "The same quarter, two years ago, was three hundred and twelve."

"A third."

"A third, and a little less." She turns the ledger so he can see the columns. Her finger moves down them with the patience of a woman who has been right about bad news all her life. "The vein is the reason, and the vein is the whole reason. Your father said three in a hundred, and the stele says three in a hundred, and I believe the stele. The terraces that fed the spirit rice are cold. The upper herb beds give half what they gave. Third Aunt moved the frostbell to the lower garden, where it grows, but it grows slowly, and nothing that grows slowly will pay a tribute."

"What is the treasury?"

"Two hundred and sixty low stones. No mid-grade." She says it quickly, the way people pull a bandage. "The last three went into your pills, and I do not regret them. But the tribute to the Sect is three hundred, and it falls due at the autumn court, and the court is in thirty days."

"Forty stones short."

"Forty stones short before we pay a single guard, a single herbalist or a single bowl of rice." Wenjun closes the ledger gently. "I could make it come out even on paper. Your second brother did that for eleven years. I prefer to tell you what the paper says."

Wenyuan looks at the ledgers, and then at the window, where the east wall stands pale against a pale sky. He has talismans in the next room that sell for a quarter stone each. He is the best talisman drawer in three valleys, and the clan's greatest source of income, and he knows exactly how many he can draw in a day, because his father made him count them for thirty years. Twelve. Fifteen, now that his hand is mended.

"What would you do?" he asks.

"I would lease the eastern terraces to the Zhao family," Wenjun says, "and I would be wrong."

He almost smiles. "Why would you be wrong?"

"Because they offered, and the price they named is exactly the price of our debts. Because a lease gives them the right to walk the eastern wall. Because it is the kind of mercy a patient man hands you before he takes your house." She taps the red cloth. "I mention it only so that you know I thought of it first and put it down."

"Thank you."

"For what?"

"For putting it down."

She looks at him a moment longer, with something in her face that is not quite pity. Then she opens the second ledger. "Now. Your father's last page."

* * *

The last page is in Lin Zhenshan's hand, a few lines in the margin of the Mirror Guard contract, written some time in the spring and never shown to anyone.

Pavilion renews at midwinter. Market warden will ask 300 as security, or give the stall to Zhao. Cannot find it. Look at the quarry spoil heaps, not at the hill. Ask the boy's teacher.

Wenyuan reads it three times.

The boy's teacher. Not Hu. Not the smith, not the old man. His father, who never in his life wrote anything he did not mean, wrote the boy's teacher, as though the relationship were the point.

He remembers something then. It is small and it does not feel important. A week before the midsummer, his father had asked him whether the spoil heaps at the head of the quarry were still being carted away. The heaps are old. They are gray gravel mixed with the black crumble that came out of the hill when Lin Shoucheng first opened the quarry for building stone. For a century the clan has thrown them down the slope and forgotten them. The children play on them.

He closes the ledger.

"Aunt Wenjun. Would you ask Old Hu to come and see me this afternoon? Not as a guest elder. Tell him I would like to ask for his advice."

"He does not give advice," Wenjun says. "He gives opinions, and then he drinks."

"Then ask him for an opinion."

* * *

The council meets at noon in the long room under the library, because it is the only room in the house with a fireplace that works, and because he cannot yet bring himself to hold it in the study.

Fourteen people sit on the benches. Third Aunt Wenqing, in plain brown, with thin hands and a thinner face; she has not lost weight so much as lost something behind her eyes. Fourth Uncle Wenshi, whose left shoulder is still bound under his tunic. Uncle Mao, with his earth-colored cloak and his bad leg stretched out on a stool. Lin Kai and Lin Dong, side-branch cousins with heavy shoulders and little to say. Lin Wenjun with her notebook. Old Nan at the far end, because the Patriarch's council has always included the oldest servant, and no one has dared to change it. And at the back, in black mourning cloth, Aunt Meirong, who was Wenhai's wife and is now nobody's anything, and who has not spoken to anyone in a hundred days.

He had not expected her to come.

He tells them the numbers. All of them, because his father would have, and because the fastest way to lose a clan is to let it discover the truth from someone else. He tells them about the third and the forty stones. When he finishes, nobody speaks for a long while.

Wenshi breaks the silence, as Wenshi always does. "The guard can take escort work. Willow Ford merchants pay four stones a trip to the border road and they are short of men. I can send ten, for ten days a month."

"Ten guards on the road are ten guards not on the wall," Mao says.

"The wall has nothing to guard against for the moment."

"It has Zhao Heng."

"Zhao Heng is lying in a bed with a hole in his dantian and a physician's hand on his wrist. Whatever he sends will be smaller than what he sent in the summer."

"Smaller," Mao says, "is not the same as nothing. I held a gate on one leg all that day. I know what nothing looks like." He says it mildly. Nobody argues with him.

"Escort work, then," Wenyuan says. "Eight guards, not ten, and none of them alone. Fourth Brother, you will choose them. Not for strength. For sense."

Wenshi nods once. He looks relieved to have been given a thing to do.

"Third Aunt."

Wenqing stirs. "The Breath-Gathering pills sell. Sect Alchemy Pavilion sells them cheaper, and everyone knows it, but a mother in Willow Ford would rather buy from a woman she can find than from a pavilion that sends a clerk. I can double the output if the herbs hold. They will not hold." She turns her cup between her hands. "I can brew from anything. I cannot brew from nothing."

"Then we find more herbs."

"Where? The outer forest has what it has. Every spirit-herb within an hour's walk is either mine or somebody else's." She looks up at last, and her eyes are tired and very clear. "I will say it, since someone has to. The hill is dying, Wenyuan. Slowly, so that nobody has to scream. I do not know how a clan holds its ground when the ground itself goes cold."

It is the first time in a hundred days anyone has said it aloud. Nobody moves.

Then Aunt Meirong speaks.

"My husband's loans," she says.

Her voice is rusty. Every head turns. She does not look at any of them. She looks at the floor, at the old boards between her black shoes, and she says the rest in one breath, like something rehearsed in the dark.

"He lent clan money to five households. The ledgers say two hundred and eighty stones outstanding. You will want it back. I would want it back." She swallows. "I am asking you not to call it in this year. Mao's house, Kai's, Dong's, Shu's, Tang's. They borrowed because he told them it was the clan's wish, and they believed him because he was the steward. If you take that money now they will have nothing. They will go to the Zhao. They will go to the first man who offers a roof." Her hands are folded so tightly the knuckles are white. "It is the only thing I can do for him. I cannot make him a good man. I can stop him from having been the cause of this too."

Lin Wenjun opens her mouth. Wenyuan raises a hand, and she closes it again.

"Aunt Meirong," he says. "Look at me."

Slowly, she does.

"The ledger says two hundred and eighty. I say the debt was never theirs. It was taken in the name of the clan by a man the clan trusted, and the clan failed to see him. If anyone owes that money it is us." He keeps his voice level. "I forgive it. All of it. I will have it written today, in my hand, and the seal will be on it. The five houses owe the clan nothing for what Wenhai did."

Wenjun makes a small, pained sound. "That is two hundred and eighty stones."

"Yes."

"We are forty stones short as it is."

"Yes." He looks at her kindly. "And in thirty days, when I stand at the autumn court and every side-branch household is behind me, I will not be forty stones short of anything that matters. A clan that Zhao cannot buy by the house is worth more than the money. I would rather be poor and whole."

For a long time nobody says anything. Then old Mao slowly stands, on his bad leg, with Kai's hand under his elbow, and bows to the Patriarch's chair. After him Kai. After him Dong. They do not make a speech. One by one the side-branch cousins stand and bow, and Aunt Meirong puts her face in her hands.

Wenyuan watches them and thinks: Father, you would have counted the stones. I know you would. I do not know if that was the wiser thing. But I think it is the thing that keeps the walls up.

He finds that his left hand has stopped shaking.

* * *

Old Hu does not come in the afternoon. Wenyuan goes to him.

The old granary stands against the east wall, with its tall doors tied open and its chimney leaning at an angle that suggests it has opinions. Black smoke rolls out from under the eaves. Inside, the air is thick with the smell of hot iron and wine. Hu stands at the anvil with his sleeve pinned and a hammer in his left hand, and at his shoulder a boy of nine is working a bellows with both arms, his thin face streaked with soot.

Jian looks up. He does not stop pumping. He nods, a small grave nod, as though his father were a customer.

"Patriarch," Hu says, without turning. "Mind the pit."

There is a pit just inside the door, about a stride wide and filled with something that smells like the bottom of a well. Wenyuan steps around it. "What is it?"

"Lin family spoil heaps," Hu says. "A hundred and thirty years of them. I took a basket on a whim, in the spring, because the boy had a theory." The hammer falls, and a ring of dull orange flies up from the metal. "Pass me the tongs, radish."

Jian passes them. Hu pulls a lump from the coals and turns it under the light. It is gray and blistered and ugly. Along one side, where it has cracked, a vein of dull yellow shows. Wenyuan has seen that color on the best spear-heads in the armory, and on nothing else.

"Spirit iron," he says.

"Poor stuff. Yellow, low. A quarter of the weight is slag, and the rest is trash that does not know it is metal." Hu drops the lump on the anvil and strikes it. A piece of the gray comes away, clean as a scab. "But it is spirit iron. That is a hundred and thirty years of Qi that the old vein spat out and nobody noticed. Those heaps are not rubbish, Patriarch. They are a mine that somebody forgot to close."

Wenyuan stares at the lump. "How much is there?"

"I have not counted. The boy says forty cartloads at the head of the quarry, more along the slope." Hu shrugs. "At the price a Willow Ford refiner pays for Yellow-low ingot, that is somewhere between four hundred stones and a great deal more. It depends on how quickly it can be done and whether anyone is watching."

"Four hundred."

"I said between. Do not give me that look. I am not the one who has to carry it."

Wenyuan turns his head, very slowly, to look at the boy at the bellows.

Jian has stopped pumping now. He stands with his hands on the wooden grip, and his face is perfectly plain, a nine-year-old's face, soot and a scab on the chin. But his eyes are steady, and they are not a child's. He is waiting. He is not afraid, but he is waiting, the way a man waits at a door he has already decided to walk through if it opens.

Ask the boy's teacher, his father wrote. Look at the quarry spoil heaps, not at the hill.

Father. Did you know?

He thinks of a hundred things. The ink on the Mirror Guards, so even. The paper. The pill that did what no pill had done in the old man's lifetime. The boy sitting up in the chamber of the stone hut, small and gray, while two Foundation Establishment cultivators fought over the door. He thinks of the question he could ask, and the answer he might receive, and what it would cost the boy to give it.

Hu is watching him. The old man's ash-gray eyes have gone very still.

"I do not need to know," Wenyuan says carefully, "how the heaps came to be on the list of things worth looking at."

"No," Hu agrees.

"I need to know whether it can be done safely."

"It can be done safely if it is done quietly. The Zhao are going to see smoke over the east wall, and they are going to ask where the iron comes from." Hu puts down the hammer. "I will tell them it is mine. I will tell them I am a drunk old refiner who found the heap and cannot stop poking it. It is even true. I have been poking it for months. They know my name from a hundred years of stories, and a man who is famous for being a fool is the safest man alive."

"The refinery will be yours."

"On paper. In practice it will pay Lin rice." The old man's mouth twists. "I do not want your stones, Patriarch. I want the boy to have something to hold when the hill is gone."

When the hill is gone. The words hang in the smoky air, and nobody contradicts them.

"The granary is yours," Wenyuan says at last. "The spoil heaps are yours to work. I will send Kai and Dong to carry, and Wenshi's guards to watch the road. Whatever comes out is the clan's, less your wine." He pauses. "And I will draw you Boundary Alarms for every door. If a stranger walks past the wall, I would like to hear of it before he does."

Hu snorts. "Wine, and not a word about what it is made from."

"I never ask a man what is in his wine."

For a moment the old artifact refiner's face does something unexpected. It is not a smile. It is the memory of one.

"You are your father's son," Hu says, and picks up his hammer.

* * *

Evening, in the Patriarch's study, with the door open and a single lamp burning.

Wenyuan has written the forgiveness and sealed it. He has signed the order for eight guards. He has drafted three Boundary Alarm slips, each in a better hand than the last, and the third is perfect. The spirit-hair brush runs over the paper without a tremor, and the Qi follows the stroke exactly the way it did when he was twenty-five, and he has to lay the brush down and sit still for a minute because his eyes have blurred.

"Father?"

Jian stands in the doorway with a tray. There is tea on it, and a bowl of rice porridge with a pale egg in the middle. He has washed his face, and there is a trace of soot left behind his ear.

"Your arm," Wenyuan says. It is the first thing he thinks of. "Is it better?"

"It is better." Jian sets the tray on the desk and flexes his right hand to show it. "Aunt Wenqing says I may use it for everything but the big hammer. I told her I do not use the big hammer. She did not believe me."

"She is wise."

"She is suspicious. It is not the same." Jian looks at the ledgers, and then at the black chair, and then at his father. "Are we in trouble?"

It is the question of a child, and Wenyuan answers it as he would answer a man. "Yes. Not today. In thirty days we will be forty stones short, and in a year we will be eighty, and in three years the hill will be as cold as the Willow Ford road. But we are not alone, and we have a few things. We have people who bowed to me today when I gave away two hundred and eighty stones." He stops. "I am not sure why I am telling a nine-year-old this."

"Because I asked."

"Yes." He rubs his eyes. "Yes. That is the reason."

Jian is quiet. Then he says, very carefully, "Hu says the heaps hold between four hundred and a great deal more. He is a careful man. If it is four hundred, we can pay the tribute and the Pavilion's security with some left over." A pause. "If it is a great deal more, we will not be poor any longer. Not rich. But not poor."

"Hu said that."

"Hu said it first." The boy's face does not change. "I only carried the baskets."

I only carried the baskets.

Wenyuan lowers his hand. He looks at his son, in the lamplight, the sooty ear, the scab on his chin and the thin, serious mouth, and sees nothing at all that he can name. Nothing that should be there is there, and nothing that should not be there is anywhere to be found. It is like looking at still water on a windless morning. The surface is perfect. He cannot see the bottom.

His father's voice comes back to him, from the day in the hall when the old man lay dying. Do not ask him what.

"Jian."

"Yes, Father?"

"I am going to ask you one question. Only one, and then I am never going to ask you another."

The boy does not move. His hands go still on the edge of the tray.

"Are you eating enough?"

A silence. It goes on a half-breath too long.

"Yes," Jian says. His voice is not quite steady. "Mother says I eat like a wolf."

"She is right." Wenyuan finds that he is smiling, and that his eyes are wet. "Go to bed. And Jian."

"Yes?"

"Thank you for the tea."

The boy picks up the tray and puts it down again, as though he has forgotten something. For a moment he looks as though he is going to say a great deal. Then he only bows, a small, exact bow, and goes out and closes the door softly behind him.

Wenyuan sits alone with the lamp, and the porridge steams, and he does not eat it for a long time.

* * *

The messenger comes at the hour of the rat, when the house is asleep.

Wenyuan is still at the desk. He hears the Boundary Alarm slip on the east wall warm and fade, which is only the late rider announcing himself, and then a quiet knock at the study door. It is Wenshi, a lamp in one hand, with a flat bamboo tube in the other.

"From Willow Ford," he says. "A Sect courier, a boy in gray. He would not leave it with the gate. He said it must be put in the Patriarch's hand." Wenshi hesitates. "It is a Registry seal."

Wenyuan takes the tube. The wax is blue, stamped with the three-cloud crest of the Outer Affairs Hall, and below the crest a smaller seal, plain and square. It is the seal of Arbiter Shen Wuye.

He breaks it and reads.

The letter is short, and written in the dry exact script of a man who has never written an unnecessary word. It confirms that the house of Lin of Green Pine Hill has completed the hundred days of mourning, as the Compact requires. It confirms that Lin Wenyuan, son of Lin Zhenshan, is recognized in his own right as Patriarch of the tributary house, and that his name will be entered in the autumn register. It offers the Hall's condolence.

Then, in a line by itself:

The house is reminded that a Patriarch recognized without a registered heir stands under the Headless House clause until an heir is named. The next opportunity to register an heir is the Spring Register at Willow Ford. The Hall observes that the last petition under this clause was received from a member of the household and was not withdrawn.

Wenyuan reads the last line twice.

Was not withdrawn.

Not Wenhai's. Wenhai is dead, and a dead man's petition lapses. This is something else, something filed afterward by another hand, on the day of the funeral perhaps, while a hill full of people was weeping. A new signature, on an old paper. Somebody in this household, or somebody who is pretending to be, has put his name to a request that the neighbor with the oldest grudge be allowed to walk in and keep order the next time a Lin Patriarch falls.

"Eldest Brother," Wenshi says carefully. "What does it say?"

"It says I must name an heir by spring, or I must not die before." He folds the letter and lays it under the lamp. "It says it very politely."

"Then name Feng."

"I will." His hand moves, and finds the dent in the arm of the chair where his father's sword hand lay. "I will name Feng, and he will go to the Outer Court in the spring with the whole clan's hope on his back. And then I will have one son who is a triple root with a spear, and one who is a pseudo-root who counts." He hears his own voice and stops it. "Forgive me. It is late."

Wenshi says nothing. He puts down the lamp, and then, awkwardly, he sets a hand on his brother's shoulder. It is the first time he has done it since the funeral.

"Whatever you have been thinking," he says, "I think you should not think it tonight."

"No. You are right." Wenyuan rubs his face. "Go to bed, Fourth Brother."

Wenshi goes. The door closes. The lamp flame leans once and straightens.

Wenyuan does not go to bed. He sits with the letter until the oil is nearly out. Then he rises, takes up the spirit-hair brush, and writes a message on a clean sheet in the best hand he has had in ten years.

To the Arbiter of the Outer Affairs Hall, at Willow Ford. From Lin Wenyuan of Green Pine Hill.

I name my son Lin Feng as heir to the house. I request that his name be entered at the Spring Register. I request, further, that the Hall tell me whose signature stands on the petition that has not been withdrawn.

He reads it over. Then he adds a last line, smaller, almost an afterthought.

Please also inform me, if it is within the Hall's knowledge, whether any person has lately made inquiries about my younger son.

He does not know why he writes it. He only knows, as he seals the letter and sets the wax down on the blue paper, that a nine-year-old brought him tea tonight and could not quite say that he was fine.

Outside, the east wall is dark, and the smoke has died away from the granary chimney. Somewhere below, at the head of the quarry, in the heaps that a century forgot, the black gravel lies cold and quiet under the autumn stars. It is very old. It is full of things nobody has looked at.

On the Patriarch's desk, among the stacks of ledgers, the lamp gutters and goes out.
